Across 4 other studies of ordinary farms and markets, reported lead means and medians on a dry-weight basis ranged from 43 µg/kg (Charles et al. 2017) to 3,160 µg/kg (Charles et al. 2017).<sup class="cite">[[sources/charles2017-instant-noodles-nigeria-risk|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Charles IA, Ogbolosingha AJ, Afia IU · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/charles2017-instant-noodles-nigeria-risk">Health risk assessment of instant noodles commonly consumed in Port Harcourt, Nigeria</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Science and Pollution Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/charles2017-instant-noodles-nigeria-risk">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, 3 studies on a dry-weight basis reported means and medians from 4 µg/kg (Kakoma et al. 2021) to 1,200 µg/kg (Kakoma et al. 2021).<sup class="cite">[[sources/kakoma2021-windhoek-instant-noodles-metals|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kakoma FIS, Awofolu OR · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kakoma2021-windhoek-instant-noodles-metals">CONTAMINATION AND HEALTH RISK ASSESSMENT OF INSTANT NOODLES BY HEAVY METALS FROM COMMERCIAL OUTLETS IN WINDHOEK, NAMIBIA</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">African Journal of Food, Agriculture, Nutrition and Development 21(7):18245-18260</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kakoma2021-windhoek-instant-noodles-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Higher results came from contaminated or exposed settings rather than ordinary supply. Noodles, as sold from retail brand C had cadmium higher at 1,300 µg/kg, against 100 µg/kg for retail brand A in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the noodles came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-noodles" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-noodles-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of noodles, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

censoring. Each source drawer identifies methods and overlapping samples. No matched reference or pooled distribution is inferred.</p></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:noodles-dc349e2cefc3:2570203f6e7e"><summary>HMI noodles Pb reference · Noodles, as sold</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:noodles-dc349e2cefc3:2570203f6e7e"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI noodles Pb reference · Noodles, as sold. Noodles, as sold; As sold, as eaten or fresh weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>≤6.2</td><td>0.6–6.6 (bounded)</td><td>400–600 (bounded)</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>≤6.2</td><td>≤7</td><td>400–2800 (bounded)</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>17 reference units; 3 sampling families. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>10</td><td>33%</td></tr><tr><td>Elsheikh et al. 2020</td><td>1</td><td>33%</td></tr><tr><td>Shaikh et al. 2025</td><td>6</td><td>33%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for noodles, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>3 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li><li><a href="../sources/elsheikh2020-toxic-trace-elements-children-foods-infant-formulae-saudi" class="internal" data-slug="sources/elsheikh2020-toxic-trace-elements-children-foods-infant-formulae-saudi" data-no-cite-meta>Elsheikh et al. 2020</a></li><li><a href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry" class="internal" data-slug="sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry" data-no-cite-meta>Shaikh et al. 2025</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. Method: hmi-pooled-reference-v2.</p><p>hmi-pooled-reference-v2:noodles-dc349e2cefc3:2570203f6e7e</p><p>The reference is computed by HMI from admitted evidence, not copied from a study baseline. It describes the evidence currently in this scope; it is not a worldwide or current-lot benchmark. Source, year and region filters do not change it. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach noodles

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach noodles comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Noodles, as sold from retail brand C had cadmium higher at 1,300 µg/kg, against 100 µg/kg for retail brand A in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

## Processing, cooking and preparation

<a id="hmi-ing-016"></a>
<a id="how-do-specified-processing-or-preparation-steps-change-the-measured-metal-endpoints"></a>

Processed or prepared forms were compared only with unprocessed noodles in the same study and group. Noodles, cooked (PAHO) had cadmium lower at 9.7 µg/kg, against 17.5 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (noodles, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Forms differ in water content, so a per-kilogram difference is not by itself a measured removal or gain of metal.

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.

<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into noodles?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, noodles from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than noodles from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Noodles, as sold from retail brand A had lead higher at 600 µg/kg, against 400 µg/kg for retail brand A in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Shaikh U, Samant R · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Quantitative Determination of Heavy Metals in Ready to Eat Food Products</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal for Multidisciplinary Research (IJFMR) 7(6), November-December 2025</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/shaikh2025-mumbai-ready-to-eat-foods-voltammetry">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-noodles" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-noodles" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in noodles?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in noodles?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, noodles, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (3.15 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (6.2 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in EMRO (16.5 µg/kg) and the highest in PAHO (54 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-noodles" data-anchor="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-noodles" data-question="Does processing change heavy metals in noodles?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does processing change heavy metals in noodles?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same noodles.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Noodles, cooked (PAHO) had cadmium lower at 9.7 µg/kg, against 17.5 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (noodles, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-noodles-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-noodles-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in noodles is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in noodles is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 4 results from 3 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Centre for Food Safety FEHD HKSAR · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">The First Hong Kong Total Diet Study: Inorganic Arsenic</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Centre for Food Safety, Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Across 2 other studies of ordinary farms and markets, reported inorganic arsenic means and medians with the basis not stated ranged from 3 µg/kg (Centre for Food Safety FEHD HKSAR 2012) to 14 µg/kg (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014).<sup class="cite">[[sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic|12]]<span
